subject.title: Song to Amarantha, that she would Dishevel her Hair
subject.author: Richard Lovelace
subject.text:
Amarantha sweet and fair
Ah braid no more that shining hair!
As my curious hand or eye
Hovering round thee let it fly.

Let it fly as unconfin'd
As its calm ravisher, the wind,
Who hath left his darling th'East,
To wanton o'er that spicy nest.

Ev'ry tress must be confest
But neatly tangled at the best;
Like a clue of golden thread,
Most excellently ravelled.

Do not then wind up that light
In ribands, and o'er-cloud in night;
Like the sun in's early ray,
But shake your head and scatter day.

See 'tis broke! Within this grove
The bower, and the walks of love,
Weary lie we down and rest,
And fan each other's panting breast.

Here we'll strip and cool our fire
In cream below, in milk-baths higher:
And when all wells are drawn dry,
I'll drink a tear out of thine eye,

Which our very joys shall leave
That sorrows thus we can deceive;
Or our very sorrows weep,
That joys so ripe, so little keep.

title: Joys So Ripe, So Little Kept
standfirst: Richard Lovelace's invitation to let her hair down reads as pure Cavalier seduction, but his own editors have long argued that Amarantha was also Lucasta, the woman he loved who married someone else after wrongly hearing Lovelace had died of a wound. By the time the poem reached print, its closing warning about joy running out had already come true.

sections.heading: A Ball of Thread Ariadne Never Meant to Tangle
sections.body: "Ah braid no more that shining hair!" is a command, not a request, and Richard Lovelace spends the next six stanzas making the case for it, working an iambic tetrameter through rhyming couplets that come loose along with the hair itself. The poem's best image compares Amarantha's undone tresses to "a clue of golden thread, / Most excellently ravelled" — a clue in the older sense, a clew, a ball of yarn, the kind Ariadne gave Theseus to find his way back out of the Cretan labyrinth. By Lovelace's time the word [already carried its modern meaning too](https://www.etymonline.com/word/clue), something that leads you to an answer. His joke is that this clue leads nowhere on purpose: a labyrinth-thread that is not wound but "most excellently ravelled." Two of the poem's stanzas were set to music by [Henry Lawes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Lawes), the court composer who wrote the songs for Milton's *Comus* — so this was not only read in private, it was sung.

sections.heading: The Book Spells Her Two Ways
sections.body: The full title of the 1649 volume, published on 14 May, is *Lucasta: Epodes, Odes, Sonnets, Songs, &c. to which is added Aramantha, A Pastoral*. The pastoral's heroine and the song's addressee are given as two different words — Aramantha against Amarantha, the two middle consonants swapped. William Carew Hazlitt, editing the poems in 1863, had no doubt they were the same figure: "no one who reads 'Amarantha, a Pastoral,' doubts that Lucasta and Amarantha are one and the same person," he wrote, treating the pastoral as proof that Lovelace's two heroines were a single woman under two names. Even Anthony Wood, the Oxford antiquary whose account of Lovelace's life underlies most later ones, could not keep the spelling straight — Hazlitt's edition notes that Wood used "Aramantha" throughout his life of the poet, a plain misprint for the name the poems themselves use.

sections.heading: A Pun His Own Editor Called Violent
sections.body: Wood's *Athenae Oxonienses*, the standard seventeenth-century account of Oxford-educated writers, says Lovelace courted "a gentlewoman of great beauty and fortune, named Lucy Sacheverell, whom he usually called Lux Casta" — chaste light — and that the nickname collapsed into Lucasta. It is a pleasing story and the one still repeated. Hazlitt didn't believe it: he called the corruption of Lucy Sacheverell into Lucasta "not very obvious, and rather violent," and guessed that "the author of the Athenae was misled by his informant on this occasion." He never extended the same doubt to Amarantha. The etymology he rejected; the identity he accepted without argument.

sections.heading: The Wound That Wasn't Fatal, and the Marriage That Was
sections.body: Lovelace fought for the French crown against Spain and was wounded at the [Siege of Dunkirk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Dunkirk_%281646%29) in the autumn of 1646, a siege that ran from early September to 11 October and ended in a Franco-Dutch victory. Word reaching England said he had died of the wound. Wood records what happened next: Lucy Sacheverell, "upon a stray report that Lovelace was dead of his wound received at Dunkirk, soon after married" someone else. Lovelace had not died — he lived over a decade more — but by the time *Lucasta* went to press in 1649, the woman it addresses as both Amarantha and its title muse had already been another man's wife for some time. Read against that timeline, the song's closing couplet stops sounding like a seduction line and starts sounding like a diagnosis: "Or our very sorrows weep, / That joys so ripe, so little keep."

sections.heading: Three Deaths for One Man
sections.body: Wood's account of the end is precise and grim: Lovelace "died in a very mean lodging in Gunpowder Alley, near Shoe Lane," and was buried at the west end of [St Bride's Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Bride%27s_Church) on Fleet Street, "in sixteen hundred fifty and eight." John Aubrey's version is vaguer but bleaker still: "Obiit in a cellar in Long acre, a little before the restauration of his Matie" — the Restoration falling in 1660. Modern reference works generally give his death as 1657 rather than Wood's 1658, one more point on which the record doesn't agree. Hazlitt, editing the poems two centuries later, pushed back hardest not on the date but on the poverty: Aubrey's own account admits that two friends, one of them named Cotton, paid Lovelace a pound a week near the end, which led Hazlitt to call the hovel story "much exaggerated and overdrawn." Nobody disputes that the marriage he might have come home to never happened. What's argued over is only how badly, and where, and in which year, he went on living without it.
